summary.title: Writing Toy Software Is A Joy
summary.one_liner: Building small "toy" programs (regex engines, emulators, interpreters, hash maps and more) with an 80:20 scope is a fast, joyful way to understand how software really works, and the post lists 25+ project ideas with difficulty and time estimates.
keywords: what i cannot create i do not understand
takeaways: Keep toy projects to roughly 20% of the work for 80% of the functionality, and avoid over-engineering.
Building small versions of tools like regex engines, hash maps, shells or interpreters builds knowledge that transfers to day-job debugging.
The post gives a list of toy projects with estimated difficulty (out of 10) and time, from a 3/10 CHIP-8 emulator to a 8/10 C-like compiler.
The author recommends working through projects without LLM solutions so the exploration stays your own.
summary.summary: The author argues that writing toy software is a joyful way to understand computing and to push back against the commodification of software development. The core advice is to keep scope minimal, let code paths crash until they must be implemented, and build your own versions of familiar tools. The bulk of the post is a list of roughly 25 toy projects (regex engine, OS kernel, emulators, interpreter, compiler, hash map, rasteriser, voxel engine, GUI toolkit, shell and more), each with an estimated difficulty and time plus suggested extensions. It closes with a recommendation to avoid LLMs for these projects and instead learn from books and exploration.
